video_title: Tracy Britt Cool: The Berkshire Model for $5–50M Businesses
transcript: [music] [music] >> Tracy said we're ready to see you. >> Yes, honored to be here. Thank you so much for having me. >> I'd love you to take me all the way back to where your first interest in investing and business came from. >> So, I grew up on a family business, a family farm, and my dad um did nothing in sort of investing except for he um invested in soybean futures to sort of hedge his position on the farm. And that was my first exposure to what it looked like, but I didn't fully understand, you know, commodity investing is a bit different than what I got interested in. But then over time when I went to college, I sort of found investing, I found Warren Buffett, I started reading a lot, and it just I naturally gravitated towards it. Building great businesses, finding companies that are undervalued, investing in them, that sort of concept resonated with me and was very early on, you know, just something natural. >> So, it's very rare that somebody picks up that material, reads it, it resonates, and then they find a way to connect with Warren. >> Yeah. >> Won't you walk me through that story, how that all happened? >> Yeah, you know, I started out just writing to investors that I admired and respected um and that I wanted to learn from. So, I actually was writing letters to, you know, um CEOs of different firms on Wall Street, and I wrote a letter to Warren asking actually to bring a group of students out to Omaha. I had started a nonprofit focused on investment education for women, and he had had uh MBA students come, but really hadn't had undergrads. And so, wrote him this letter and he generously said yes, and we brought a group of students out to Omaha. >> So, what happened from there? >> So, got to know him just a little bit through it um and planned that trip I think three or four times. And then when I graduated business school, wrote him another letter, asked if I could come out a day, a week, a month and pick his brain, fully assuming he'd say no, but fortunately [laughter] he said yes. Uh so, I spent my post MBA summer working with him. And then at the end of summer, he said, "I'd love to hire you, just don't have a role." You know, Berkshire's 25 people uh at headquarters, so very small. I started my full-time job and he called a few weeks later and said if you're interested, I'll create a role for you to join. So, obviously quickly quit my job and moved out to Omaha later that year. >> And what do you think it was or maybe what did he tell you after the fact because it it's so rare that that would have happened if at all? >> Yeah, I think Warren, you know, he's always been very open at keeping and and bringing people into his life at different stages. You know, he was nearly 80 when I joined Berkshire. So, to trust me at that age was really you know, something special. And I never asked him specifically why, but I think it was probably a combination of you grit, resiliency, willingness to work hard, you know, personality, those sort of dynamics that came together. And it's funny, I had a number of people over the years write me letters and occasionally they stood out to me, too. All right? And my partner Brian Humphrey wrote me a letter when he was in Stanford at business school and that's how I met him. And you for some reason that letter resonated with me and what he was doing so I think it's one of those things that's like hard to put your finger on it, but you know it when you see it. >> So, if you're giving advice to people who are asking you about how to approach someone that they admire, is there anything that you've been able to pull from the ones that resonated for you? >> Yeah, I think a couple things. One is you obviously want to try to find a mutual connection. You're from the same town, you're interested in similar things or you went to the same school, same interest, those types of thing I think really resonate. And then I think just being humble, being yourself, you know, definitely not using AI to generate it, not sending the same letter to 30 people, you know, really customizing it. And I found like handwritten letters or you know, at least physical letters were far more impactful than sending emails or you know, connecting on LinkedIn just because that's so per se pervasive these days, it doesn't really stand out. >> So, when you showed up at Omaha, what was the job as the 26th employee? >> Yeah, so I was really Warren's sort of chief of staff. So, I spent time working on anything that crossed his desk. So, looking at investments, I worked on insurance deals, or acquisitions, um a variety of things. Um and it was just an opportunity for me to learn and grow, uh which was really remarkable. >> What did that feel like day-to-day? >> There was a lot of responsibility where and I sort of joked, you know, Warren had, you know, quite a few IQ points on me as well as 50 years of experience. So, I had a lot to catch up on. And so, I spent a lot of time reading, learning, working late, you know, trying to really understand our businesses at Berkshire, why we invested in them, what worked, what didn't work. And Warren was very gracious spending time with me, going to lunch, and really talking about those companies in detail. And that just helped me become a better investor, much more thoughtful in what I was doing. And then the day-to-day work was, you know, really what was coming across his desk. So, it varied widely, but it was going deep on on a variety of topics that there was some need or some interest on the Berkshire side. >> How did your time there transition from pure investing to that alongside of jumping into some of the portfolio companies? >> Yeah, so when I was at Berkshire, I would travel and, you know, just over time meet some of the companies. And Warren started asking me my thoughts on the businesses. And so, the first was Larson Jewel, which is a custom framing business. Then there was Benjamin Moore, Oriental Trading Company, Johns Manville, and others. And as I did that, Warren started asking me to come in in an a chairman role. And typically, those businesses were were ones where the company wasn't operating to its full potential. And so, there was just opportunity to help it. And so, I'd come alongside management team to really help them figure that out and navigate it. In some cases, changing out the management team to sort of help support that. And that was sort of my first foray into operating. As I did that, what I really realized was that there was going to be more value created on the operating side going forward. In the buyout world, the days of buying businesses for seven times and selling them for 12 a few years later was probably gone. And you actually really needed to add more value. But that being said, very few operators in buyout, venture I think is quite different, but in buyout actually have operating experience. And so, I thought to myself, if I, you know, am an investor, but I go get operating experience, I'll be a much better investor. I'll have more credibility, more empathy, more ability to sort of help these businesses. And so that really was the turning point in my mind of this sort of power and this shift that was happening in investing and operating. >> I'd love you to walk me through a story or two in your time at Berkshire of those operating roles. What you saw when you got there, how you were able to make change. >> Yeah, so if you look at like Benjamin Moore, I was uh chair of that business. Benjamin Moore is an amazing brand. It had been built built over a hundred plus years. Um really special, really tangible, sold through dealer network. But over a 10-year period, it had really lost its way. Volume growth in terms of gallons had come down considerably. Earnings were relatively flat, but what was happening was the business was sort of cutting marketing spend and sort of taking price to sort of maintain earnings instead of really investing in the channel, investing in marketing, investing in the brand, which is critical in that type of business. And so when I joined, it really was this opportunity to say, "Okay, how do we reinvest in the core part of the business?" And if we do that well, we can sort of reposition the stores as leaders in their space. We can reinvest in our dealers and see the specialness of that. Over sort of the time, we significantly improved the earnings of the business while strengthening the channel and driving it through earnings or through um volume growth, not just, you know, uh financial engineering, so to speak. So what did you see from going into the company to help them do that that was different from seeing on paper that they had decreased marketing spend and there was less of a sell-through as a result? Yeah, so I think going into a business, it's really understanding what are the key drivers, what is influencing management in their decisions and what they're doing. In that situation, it was just this goal to maintain earnings that they were focused on. So their incentives were misaligned. So they were focused on how do I retain earnings versus how do I reinvest in the future of the business? And so in doing that, then it became clear like, "Oh, we need to reinvest in the future. What does that look like?" And in a business like that, brand is so incredibly important. So getting awareness, visibility, that connection. So and they had cut brand spending and marketing spend. So there was an opportunity there. The second is the store experience. When you walk into a store, what does it feel like from a customer? So always starting with that customer, like what does that look like, and how can we improve it? And then the lastly I would say is always culture. You know, there's often times in these organizations where if they've declined, there's a cultural element that's got off that's got off track. Um in that case, it becomes sort of stagnant, they were afraid to make decisions, they weren't leaving the building. And so there was an opportunity to reinvigorate the culture to sort of help support those those first two things. >> In that example, what did you learn about what had happened over those 10 years that hadn't been in place before that led to that period of time where you could change the inflection back up? >> Yeah, so it really is going back and understanding and asking questions. Why did we do this? Why didn't we do this? What was happening along the way? And I find when sometimes you take a step back and look at like a 10-year period, you can actually see stuff that each year you don't see. When you're looking at a business each year, it's just a little decline, a little decline, and you're like, "Oh, we just, you know, maybe it was the market, maybe it was some conditions, maybe it was an anomaly." So you don't really take ownership of a decline. But when you look at 10 over 10 years and your volume's declined, you know, 10 plus percent, then you're like, "Oh wow, there's something serious going on here." And so then you start to dig in and say, "Why is that happening?" And really look at those next level. And you can look at others in the market, you Sherwin-Williams had done a great job during this time period as an example, and saying, "Okay, what was happening?" And then what do we need to go figure out to improve that? And I think in this case, it was a lot of the incentives were misaligned, you they were focusing on retaining earnings versus growing volume and growing the business. Um and they had sort of focused on um the wrong part of the the dealer like in the relationship and the experience. So they sort of felt like the dealer was waning and so they started shifting away from the dealer instead of like leaning into the dealer. And so, they were actually exploring other partnerships with big boxes at the time and that just really wasn't the right strategy for this brand. And so, just helping coming in re-centering, refocusing. And the reality when doing that is usually the answer is in the building. You know, people know what that needs to be done and how to do it. It's just either you're not getting to it or you're not listening to it or something else is influencing the decisions that's like leading to the wrong outcome. >> So, when you look at that example in the context of everything you did at Berkshire, how did you think about managing your time? >> Yeah. So, you know, Warren always said like if you want something done give it to a busy person and right it like it'll get done over time. And so, I just took on more and more. So, starting on the investing side and then became chair of each of these businesses, kept those roles when I became CEO of Pampered Chef, really wanted to go get operating experience and I think when you're um doing a lot you really start to realize what's most critical and how do you prioritize and how do you focus? And I think that ends up being what's most interesting in a business is that usually there's three to four things that really matter and we get stuck doing all of these different things. And the same thing goes with an investment. Usually there's three or four things that really matter and you know, we have a 100-page deck that goes through all these other items, but if you know those three to four things, you really spend your time on those and you can get them right, then the likelihood that you're successful is much greater. So, I think with time is just really focusing on the things that matter most um that are going to move the needle. >> And how about the distinction in your time from being chairman of several companies and then CEO at Pampered Chef? >> Yeah. So, when I was chair, what I really realized was, you know, there is this opportunity to help management teams and support them, but it actually if you've never been in the shoes, you're just always a step behind because they're like, "Well, yeah, that sounds great, but you've never actually done this." And so, what I realized was more and more value be created on that operating side. You needed to drive real earnings growth in businesses. And so, if I could go be a CEO and get that operating experience, I would just have much more experience that would help me in the future with investing or working with management teams. So, I went to Warren and said, you know, I'd like to be CEO of, you know, Pampered Chef, which I was working with at the time. And then what I saw was there's a lot of opportunity in that business. It had a strong brand. It had a strong channel. It just had been under managed. And so, the transition from chairman to CEO was really, I think for a lot of people, surprising, right? Very seldom do you see investors go into operating roles. Um but for me, I really felt like it was going to be the future of investing was going to be operating, and I would be a much better investor if I went and got that experience directly um and gained that credibility, the empathy, the connection with these leaders that would resonate with sellers in the future, resonate with management teams, and definitely have seen that play out at Cambrek, as well. >> As you look at those different um connections with the company from investor to chairman to CEO, how did you think about going in for the first time and laying out communicating what a plan would be? >> Yeah, so I always think the best way to go in is to go in open-minded with more questions than answers. I think investors usually come in with answers. Here's our 90-day plan. This is what we're going to go do. And I think the reality is you don't actually get the best outcomes in doing that. We as we start at Cambrek with like listen and learning. You know, how do you actually listen to people in the organization? How do you understand what's going on? How do you ask the questions that are going to help you be smarter, but also further the conversation? And if you do that well, you actually get to a better outcome. You can co-create something that's really meaningful in terms of the strategy and the direction and the focus. And that is far more powerful than coming in with a plan or a direction in what you're doing. >> What was different from what you expected at Pampered Chef? >> When I came in, I had been working with the business for about a year. So, I'd spent time learning, listening, and I had a pretty strong view at that stage of like what we needed to go do. And I told Warren it would take me a year, maybe 2 years to get this thing like really humming. You know, it had been in decline for about a decade, so it was a big turnaround that I needed to go do. And it ended up taking you nearly 4 years to do it. And the reality is is I think everything is harder in operating than it seems. And so, even though I knew what needed to go be done, I had the strategy in my mind, I knew I needed to go get the people on board, build the culture, it's a lot harder than you expect. And usually that's because it's all involved people, and people are really tough, right? You hire the wrong people, you've got to change them out. Or you've got to work on culture and retention, which that doesn't get changed overnight if, you know, you've had challenges in that in the past. And then you've got to go invest in people getting up to speed and learning sort of new tools, new practices, new spaces, and then you've got to build all this together. And so, to me that was a huge surprise, very humbling, but I think it's probably actually not dissimilar from how most investors think, right? Like, "Oh, let's take margins from 10% to 14%." You know, that's one click in my spreadsheet, but in reality in a business, that takes a lot more work to actually go do. And there's a lot of missteps or mistakes and learnings along the way to get to there. >> So, as you progress, you spend this time as a CEO, you can imagine being at Berkshire for a career, and just going in and working with different companies, larger companies, Berkshire. At what point time did you decide you wanted to go do your own thing instead of doing it within Berkshire? >> Yeah, so I was nearing sort of the conclusion of the turnaround at Pampered Chef. We had the business in a good place. I had met my now co-founder Brian Humphrey, he had joined me as CFO there. We were very well aligned from a vision and values perspective. And what I saw at that sort of stage was I could be at Berkshire forever. I'd have an amazing time there. It's a remarkable company, there's nothing like it, and I don't think there ever will be. But it was getting very big in terms of capital. So, it had 150 billion in cash at the time, you know, now it's 300 billion plus. It's very hard to move the needle with that size of check. And what I saw was actually what Berkshire had done 30 or 40 years ago was actually more interesting to me. Buying businesses like Benjamin Moore or others, where you could actually partner with them, help them accelerate the growth. And also what I've seen in the market at the time was there was just a growing group of families and founders who wanted something different. They didn't want to sell to traditional private equity. They wanted a Berkshire-like home, but they were just too small. And so there was this opportunity like in that moment to build something that was unique and different that I think was solving a pain point. And so for me it was, yes, I could stay here and be happy and probably forever, but there's also this opportunity to build something special and unique that you know I think was was really sort of differentiated in the moment. >> When Brian and you decided you're going to do this, what did you lay out as the core tenets of your philosophy having pulled from your experiences at Berkshire? >> Yeah, there were a few things that resonated with us that really were important. One is long-term thinking and a long-term structure. So I think often times long-term thinking conflicts with structure and so having those two things together was very important to us. And that very much was you know paramount to Berkshire and I think very unique and special and something we wanted to replicate at Cambrek. Second was providing sort of that operating lens and that operating expertise. So we had built what is now the Cambrek business system from the ground up learning from greats like Marmon and Toyota and Trans Diamond others and really taking those and re-sort of applying them for mid-size companies. And that tenant of that investor operator mindset in partnership was really powerful. And then lastly was just this partnership mindset of like working with families and founders and coming alongside them. I think so much in traditional private equity is you know we you get told what to do or you know go drive this or hit this you know plan versus how do we co-create and build something special and unique. And that partnership mentality is like so core and critical to how to how we operate and how we think. >> What did you do different structurally from the way private equity traditionally runs? >> Yeah, so we did a longer-term structure. So, you know, it has a longer-term horizon, which is beneficial for us. We have 15 plus years in our structure. And the benefit of that is that one, it self-selects investors who are long-term and oriented long-term oriented, which is very beneficial. And it's unique for owners. So, owners who say, "Look, I'm you concerned with the the three to four-year treadmill of private equity." It gives them comfort that their business isn't going to be sold bought and sold and bought and sold so sort of quickly. And it's that longer-term horizon that allows our management teams to really focus on how do I build this business for decades, not how do I build this business for a quick flip. >> And what did you find when you went into the market with that structure? >> Yes, from an investor perspective, you know, it's obviously there's some investors it just isn't a fit for. Like it doesn't match their structure, their duration, their liquidity needs, which we understand. Um but I think what it really we really saw is there was a a group of investors who were immediately resonated with them. And it was aligned with how they think about building businesses as well, which was natural. And what we said to investors is it doesn't mean you won't get any capital along the way. So, you know, there's always going to be opportunities. Um our businesses we don't put a lot a lot of leverage on them. Um and so there'll be some businesses that we exit, but a lot of our businesses will generate a fair amount of cash because they don't have a lot of leverage. And then we can return capital. We have a business JAM test. We've owned it three years. You know, we forexed the earnings in the business over that period and then we just sort of returned um you know, our initial capital to investors. And we still own our 70% you know, plus of the business. And so that I think is a great model where yes, there's liquidity. It's not the same as an exit, but that business is compounding at 20% plus a year. We'd rather continue to own that business rather than sort of exit it. >> How did you take the long-term nature of the structure and tell a story to the people you wanted to partner with? So, it could be the families, it could be the investors um to really encapsulate that idea of partnership? >> there's a few things that we highlight is as the structure is important, but it's one part of like the three-legged stool. So, there's a long-term structure that allows us to invest in these high-quality businesses. There's our Cambre community, which is how we get to know companies and we build relationships over the long term. And then there's the business system about as we add value. And they all get mutually reinforced and powerful together. So, by having that longer term structure, our management teams can think longer term. By our management teams thinking longer term, we can drive above-average returns. By having our Cambre business system, we can use it in our community. By having that in our community, we get to know owners and CEOs well ahead of any potential partnership. And when those things start to really compound on each other, you get the real value of it. And so, for us, it has been tough to like communicate that story because it's not a simple easy one. It actually is very interconnected. But our belief and our competitive advantage is it is those things, and that becomes stronger and stronger over time and harder for someone else to come in and replicate. >> the Cambre community. What did you build to generate that community? >> Yeah, so when I started as CEO of Pampered Chef, it was very lonely. I had to go out and, you know, meet with owners and and meet with other executives to really understand, how do you manage a business effectively and well? And when I was doing that, I thought, "Wow, it'd be so great to have a resource, someone who could come alongside me and say, 'This is what a great strategic planning process looks like, or this is how you can improve your executive hiring skills.'" And so, when I started sort of that journey, I really realized that there was this need to help owners, that they wanted to learn and grow, and CEOs in particular. And so, when started Cambre, we sort of brought that idea forward with this opportunity to get to know owners and CEOs over time. And so, we built the Cambre community to be sort of that home that we wanted to have in terms of learning and growing together. You know, now we have 4,000 CEOs in the community and owners and C-suite executives, where we're helping them with their business. We're really taking a step back and saying, you know, this is what a great KPI process looks like. These are what the best benchmarks are. And that community relationship has been really powerful and helpful for us because we learn about new spaces, we get to know businesses, but most importantly, these companies get to know us. And we build trust and credibility. And the reality is my view is that the world is becoming much more focused on relationship investing than sort of transaction. So, all of our investments have come through direct relationships. Um four of our seven have come through the community, but what we're doing is we're building goodwill, we're building trust. And even if the companies aren't ever going to take a partner or not interested in a partner, what we find is they become great ambassadors for us. And so, they share, you know, about Cambrek with their friends, other CEOs. And that's been been incredibly powerful. >> It's easy to see how that would work at 4,000. How do you get from zero to 4,000? >> It's a great question. So, we started with our first program called Build with Cambrek. Uh CEOs applied to it, and in our first cohort, we had five CEOs we selected, and we really over 3 months helped them in their business. Those first five CEOs recommended other CEOs. We went out to our network and started inviting them. At the end of our first year in 2021, we had 127 CEOs. So, it was still very nascent at that stage, but it really started to grow. So, we went from 127 to 500 to 1,000 to 2 to 3. And what we found is that when you do an add value, then it becomes much more of a referral community where people are inviting other people. And now we've extended the programs. So, we have that 3-month program, but we also have a 3-week masterclass where you can go deep on hiring. We'll do three 90-minute sessions and help you in hiring. We have webinars every month on different topics. Like we just did one on mission-critical roles. How do you think about mission-critical roles in your business? And you know, you know, what does that look like? And then we started doing local and national events where we bring people together in different communities in person so they can connect with other leaders in, you know, their their regions or in their areas. And that has be become more and more of a compounding nature where the relationships become stronger, our connections become, you know, more powerful, and we get to build this trust with these individuals. Um so, it's been a journey, but it's been amazing to see the power of that um and how many, you know, people engage in it, but also how much they share and bring other people into the community. >> What's the breadth of what you've taught to these CEOs through the community? >> Yeah, we really start with our business system, which is really focused on how do you manage a mid-size company? So, it starts with people. How do you attract, develop, and engage talent? So, that's everything from mission-critical roles and hiring to talent engagement, you know, communications, town halls, to incentive plans, and then development, you know, how do you develop and talent and talent talent development, career planning, um career mapping, those types of conversations. And then we have the operating system, which really falls into, you know, how do you build a plan? So, what's your strategy? How do you resource that plan? How do you think about capital allocation? How do you think about KPIs, budgeting, all of those dynamics and how you manage a business? Then we have, you know, sort of operational excellence. How do you continually get better and have better use of, you know, assets, your cost, um anything that you have sort of supporting the business. And then growth. Where's the growth in your business and what does that look like? So, that's the core of where we spend our time. And that's that helps, you know, probably probably 80% plus of companies. They struggle with, you know, topics within that um on in their respective businesses. Each business is different, but for one it might be hiring, for another it might be KPIs, but we're helping them in that. And then there's other topics we've expanded out, you know, just by demand. How do I think about M&A in my business? How do I think about developing a board in my company? How do I think about AI and the future of that? How do I think about tariffs? So, we've led, you know, round table sessions as those topics come up on those um areas. And we're sharing our own experience and perspectives, but we're also sort of getting best practices and learnings across the cohort and across the group. And so, the broader community is also sharing, and we learn a lot, you know, with people who are really at the forefront of what they're doing in their industry or on a specific topic. >> How have you um nurtured and and cultivated the community once you've built it to that many people to make sure that people stay engaged? >> Yeah, so I think for us there's the standard, you know, we offer this every month we put a written brief out on topics that we're covering that we think are helpful. The sessions that we're hosting virtually and in person that have those touchpoints. And then beyond that, it's really those personal touches, you know, we're thinking about you. We know that you told us you were focused on hiring and that was a tough challenge. Here's some new material as it relates to that. Um also, like really understanding where people are and touching base with them and connecting. And everyone, you know, struggling with something different in their business. So, as we get to know them, we can be more helpful in doing that. And then making connections. So, it might be you're looking for a board member and the space, oh, we know that we have five community members who are also, you know, in that space who might be potential board members or know someone. So, facilitating those introductions, connections also sort of further like um strengthens the power of the community. >> So, as a small firm, how do you scale your resources to be able to deliver that type of customized experience across so many people? >> Yeah, so we are try to be really thoughtful with our team. It's everyone's job to help support the community, participate in events and what we're doing. It's core to how we operate and how we think, and so that becomes really second nature to everyone in what we're doing. And then we're just really thoughtful about how to do it. So, it's not we're going to do everything, but we're going to be really focused. Once we build the muscle, it becomes easier, and then it becomes more scalable. And so, Build with CaMBRIC, you know, the first program we launched, you know, 5 years ago, we constantly improve it, but the core stays the same. And so, yes, we have a new cohort and new members, but we're not changing everything constantly, and that allows us to scale and add on, you know, more um specific programs and initiatives that are really meeting, you know, our leaders and our CEOs where they are. >> So, I'd love to turn to how you leverage that into your investing. Um you have all these people now in your network. What have you decided that you're looking for of the companies that you may want to buy? >> Yeah, so we start off big picture on what we're looking for, which is industrial services, manufacturing, some consumer. And really what we're focused on are high-quality businesses. We're looking at businesses that are 5 to 50 million in earnings, but probably what's most important and more important than the sector is just the business model. Does it have a moat? Does it have a competitive advantage? Can we see it quantitatively, and then qualitatively, can we really understand what's happening with that moat? And so that's what we're focused on and what we're looking for. Anyone can join the community who has a business over 10 million in revenue, a CEO of 10 million revenue can join. And so by doing that, what we're seeing is we have a lot of people who aren't in our target space or what we're looking for, and we're completely happy to have them join the community. But with the people that we get to know and that we're, you know, are interested in their businesses or they're interested in a potential partner, we just spend more and more time with them. And our view in the world is that, you know, the days of auctions, it's very transactional. It's not how most people think about their businesses. If you built your business over decades or it's a family business or you're founder, the idea of selling it through an auction doesn't resonate with a lot of people. You really care about your employees, you care about the future of your business, and maybe price is important, but it may not be the only thing that's important to you. It's the future value creation, it's, you know, your legacy, it's the how you're going to focus on customers. And I think that we're actually under invested in that you know, as a society and there'll be this great opportunity to invest in that more. >> Which two people have had the biggest impact on your professional life? >> You know, in hands down Warren you know, had a tremendous impact um Warren Buffett had a tremendous impact on me, you know, both in terms of giving me an opportunity when you know, I had little experience, but then just the trust and confidence that he had in me over time and the types of opportunities that he gave me um were really uh impressive. And the other I'd say is my husband, you know, definitely has affected my personal life and our family life, but even more so like my professional career. I think you know, it is especially important that the person you marry is supportive of what you're doing. I think especially for women, it's the most important career decision. Is do you have a supportive partner who can be there as a sounding board and can help you um but also flexible and willing to um to you know, believe in you. And my husband Scott has been that that and more. I couldn't have done like what I've done without him and his support. So, those would be the two I'd say. >> What's a life lesson you wish you learned earlier in life? >> Learned so many over life over my life and the like pain points of them, but I think probably one would be when you really trust and believe in people and you help them, you can get more so out of anybody than like if you are too involved, too overriding, too micromanaging. And Warren believed in me and I saw that like trust, but I I've seen it even more so in the work that I've done. But wish I would have learned that even sooner. >> Tracy, last one. If the next five years are a chapter in your life, what's that chapter about? >> It's about building. You know, and I think about us at Cambric as we're builders. We're building something special and unique, you know, for this next generation of companies, you know, investors and leaders in what we're doing. And I think this first chapter has been building the foundation and you know, now we have a very strong foundation. It's like what we can build from here. So, the next chapter for me is definitely building. >> Tracy, wishing you all the best of luck to continue building what you've already built upon. >> Thank you, Ted. >> Tracy said we're ready to see you.
>> Yes, honored to be here. Thank you so
much for having me.
>> I'd love you to take me all the way back
to where your first interest in
investing and business came from.
>> So, I grew up on a family business, a
family farm, and my dad um did nothing
in sort of investing except for he um
invested in soybean futures to sort of
hedge his position on the farm. And that
was my first exposure to what it looked
like, but I didn't fully understand, you
know, commodity investing is a bit
different than what I got interested in.
But then over time when I went to
college, I sort of found investing, I
found Warren Buffett, I started reading
a lot, and it just I naturally
gravitated towards it. Building great
businesses, finding companies that are
undervalued, investing in them, that
sort of concept resonated with me and
was very early on, you know, just
something natural.
>> So, it's very rare that somebody picks
up that material, reads it, it
resonates,
and then they find a way to connect with
Warren.
>> Yeah.
>> Won't you walk me through that story,
how that all happened?
>> Yeah, you know, I started out just
writing to investors that I admired and
respected um and that I wanted to learn
from. So, I actually was writing letters
to, you know, um
CEOs of different firms on Wall Street,
and I wrote a letter to Warren asking
actually to bring a group of students
out to Omaha. I had started a nonprofit
focused on investment education for
women, and he had had uh MBA students
come, but really hadn't had undergrads.
And so, wrote him this letter and he
generously said yes, and we brought a
group of students out to Omaha.
>> So, what happened from there?
>> So, got to know him just a little bit
through it um and planned that trip I
think three or four times. And then when
I graduated business school, wrote him
another letter, asked if I could come
out a day, a week, a month and pick his
brain, fully assuming he'd say no, but
fortunately [laughter] he said yes.
Uh so, I spent my post MBA summer
working with him. And then at the end of
summer, he said, "I'd love to hire you,
just don't have a role." You know,
Berkshire's 25 people uh at
headquarters, so very small. I started
my full-time job and he called a few
weeks later and said if you're
interested, I'll create a role for you
to join. So, obviously quickly quit my
job and moved out to Omaha
later that year.
>> And what do you think it was or maybe
what did he tell you after the fact
because it it's so rare that that would
have happened if at all?
>> Yeah, I think Warren, you know, he's
always been very open at keeping and and
bringing people into his life at
different stages. You know, he was
nearly 80 when I joined Berkshire.
So, to trust me at that age was really
you know, something special. And I never
asked him specifically why, but I think
it was probably a combination of you
grit, resiliency, willingness to work
hard, you know, personality,
those sort of dynamics that came
together. And it's funny, I had a number
of people over the years write me
letters and occasionally they stood out
to me, too. All right? And my partner
Brian Humphrey wrote me a letter when he
was in Stanford at business school and
that's how I met him. And you for some
reason that letter resonated with me
and what he was doing so I think it's
one of those things that's like hard to
put your finger on it, but you know it
when you see it.
>> So, if you're giving advice to people
who are asking you about how to approach
someone that they admire, is there
anything that you've been able to pull
from the ones that resonated for you?
>> Yeah, I think a couple things. One is
you obviously want to try to find a
mutual connection. You're from the same
town, you're interested in similar
things or you went to the same school,
same interest, those types of thing I
think really resonate. And then I think
just being humble, being yourself, you
know, definitely not using AI to
generate it, not sending the same letter
to 30 people, you know, really
customizing it. And I found like
handwritten letters or you know, at
least physical letters were far more
impactful than sending emails or you
know, connecting on LinkedIn just
because that's so per se pervasive these
days, it doesn't really stand out.
>> So, when you showed up at Omaha, what
was the job as the 26th employee?
>> Yeah, so I was really Warren's sort of
chief of staff. So, I spent time working
on anything that crossed his desk. So,
looking at investments, I worked on
insurance deals, or acquisitions, um a
variety of things. Um and it was just an
opportunity for me to learn and grow, uh
which was really remarkable.
>> What did that feel like day-to-day?
>> There was a lot of responsibility where
and I sort of joked, you know, Warren
had, you know, quite a few IQ points on
me as well as 50 years of experience.
So, I had a lot to catch up on. And so,
I spent a lot of time reading, learning,
working late, you know, trying to really
understand our businesses at Berkshire,
why we invested in them, what worked,
what didn't work. And Warren was very
gracious spending time with me, going to
lunch, and really talking about those
companies in detail. And that just
helped me become a better investor, much
more thoughtful in what I was doing. And
then the day-to-day work was, you know,
really what was coming across his desk.
So, it varied widely, but it was going
deep on on a variety of topics that
there was some need or some interest on
the Berkshire side.
>> How did your time there transition from
pure investing to that alongside of
jumping into some of the portfolio
companies?
>> Yeah, so when I was at Berkshire, I
would travel and, you know, just over
time meet some of the companies. And
Warren started asking me my thoughts on
the businesses. And so, the first was
Larson Jewel, which is a custom framing
business. Then there was Benjamin Moore,
Oriental Trading Company, Johns
Manville, and others. And as I did that,
Warren started asking me to come in in
an a chairman role. And typically, those
businesses were were ones where the
company wasn't operating to its full
potential. And so, there was just
opportunity to help it. And so, I'd come
alongside management team to really help
them figure that out and navigate it. In
some cases, changing out the management
team to sort of help support that. And
that was sort of my first foray into
operating. As I did that, what I really
realized was that there was going to be
more value created on the operating side
going forward. In the buyout world, the
days of buying businesses for seven
times and selling them for 12 a few
years later was probably gone. And you
actually really needed to add more
value. But that being said, very few
operators in buyout, venture I think is
quite different, but in buyout actually
have operating experience. And so, I
thought to myself, if I, you know, am an
investor, but I go get operating
experience, I'll be a much better
investor. I'll have more credibility,
more empathy, more ability to sort of
help these businesses. And so that
really was the turning point in my mind
of this sort of power and this shift
that was happening in investing and
operating.
>> I'd love you to walk me through a story
or two in your time at Berkshire of
those operating roles. What you saw when
you got there, how you were able to make
change.
>> Yeah, so if you look at like Benjamin
Moore, I was uh chair of that business.
Benjamin Moore is an amazing brand. It
had been built built over a hundred plus
years. Um really special, really
tangible, sold through dealer network.
But over a 10-year period, it had really
lost its way. Volume growth in terms of
gallons had come down considerably.
Earnings were relatively flat, but what
was happening was the business was sort
of cutting marketing spend and sort of
taking price to sort of maintain
earnings instead of really investing in
the channel, investing in marketing,
investing in the brand, which is
critical in that type of business. And
so when I joined, it really was this
opportunity to say, "Okay, how do we
reinvest in the core part of the
business?" And if we do that well, we
can sort of reposition the stores as
leaders in their space. We can reinvest
in our dealers and see the specialness
of that. Over sort of the time, we
significantly improved the earnings of
the business while strengthening the
channel and driving it through earnings
or through um volume growth, not just,
you know,
uh financial engineering, so to speak.
So what did you see from going into the
company to help them do that that was
different from seeing on paper that they
had decreased marketing spend and there
was less of a sell-through as a result?
Yeah, so I think going into a business,
it's really understanding what are the
key drivers, what is influencing
management in their decisions and what
they're doing. In that situation, it was
just this goal to maintain earnings that
they were focused on. So their
incentives were misaligned. So they were
focused on how do I retain earnings
versus how do I reinvest in the future
of the business? And so in doing that,
then it became clear like, "Oh, we need
to reinvest in the future. What does
that look like?" And in a business like
that, brand is so incredibly important.
So getting awareness, visibility, that
connection. So and they had cut brand
spending and marketing spend. So there
was an opportunity there. The second is
the store experience. When you walk into
a store, what does it feel like from a
customer? So always starting with that
customer, like what does that look like,
and how can we improve it? And then the
lastly I would say is always culture.
You know, there's often times in these
organizations where if they've declined,
there's a cultural element that's got
off that's got off track. Um in that
case, it becomes sort of stagnant, they
were afraid to make decisions, they
weren't leaving the building. And so
there was an opportunity to reinvigorate
the culture to sort of help support
those those first two things.
>> In that example, what did you learn
about what had happened over those 10
years that hadn't been in place before
that led to that period of time where
you could change the inflection back up?
>> Yeah, so it really is going back and
understanding and asking questions. Why
did we do this? Why didn't we do this?
What was happening along the way? And I
find when sometimes you take a step back
and look at like a 10-year period, you
can actually see stuff that each year
you don't see. When you're looking at a
business each year, it's just a little
decline, a little decline, and you're
like, "Oh, we just, you know, maybe it
was the market, maybe it was some
conditions, maybe it was an anomaly." So
you don't really take ownership of a
decline. But when you look at 10 over 10
years and your volume's declined, you
know, 10 plus percent, then you're like,
"Oh wow, there's something serious going
on here." And so then you start to dig
in and say, "Why is that happening?" And
really look at those next level. And you
can look at others in the market, you
Sherwin-Williams had done a great job
during this time period as an example,
and saying, "Okay, what was happening?"
And then what do we need to go figure
out to improve that? And I think in this
case, it was a lot of the incentives
were misaligned, you they were focusing
on retaining earnings versus growing
volume and growing the business. Um and
they had sort of focused on um the wrong
part of the the dealer like in the
relationship and the experience. So they
sort of felt like the dealer was waning
and so they started shifting away from
the dealer instead of like leaning into
the dealer. And so, they were actually
exploring other partnerships with big
boxes at the time and that just really
wasn't the right strategy for this
brand. And so, just helping coming in
re-centering, refocusing. And the
reality when doing that is usually the
answer is in the building. You know,
people know what that needs to be done
and how to do it. It's just either
you're not getting to it or you're not
listening to it or something else is
influencing the decisions that's like
leading to the wrong outcome.
>> So, when you look at that example in the
context of everything you did at
Berkshire,
how did you think about managing your
time?
>> Yeah. So, you know, Warren always said
like if you want something done give it
to a busy person and right it like it'll
get done over time. And so, I just took
on more and more. So, starting on the
investing side and then became chair of
each of these businesses, kept those
roles when I became CEO of Pampered
Chef, really wanted to go get operating
experience and I think when you're um
doing a lot you really start to realize
what's most critical and how do you
prioritize and how do you focus? And I
think that ends up being what's most
interesting in a business is that
usually there's three to four things
that really matter and we get stuck
doing all of these different things. And
the same thing goes with an investment.
Usually there's three or four things
that really matter and you know, we have
a 100-page deck that goes through all
these other items, but if you know those
three to four things, you really spend
your time on those and you can get them
right, then the likelihood that you're
successful is much greater. So, I think
with time is just really focusing on the
things that matter most um that are
going to move the needle.
>> And how about the distinction in your
time from being chairman of several
companies and then CEO at Pampered Chef?
>> Yeah. So, when I was chair, what I
really realized was, you know, there is
this opportunity to help management
teams and support them, but it actually
if you've never been in the shoes,
you're just always a step behind because
they're like, "Well, yeah, that sounds
great, but you've never actually done
this." And so, what I realized was more
and more value be created on that
operating side. You needed to drive real
earnings growth in businesses. And so,
if I could go be a CEO and get that
operating experience, I would just have
much more experience that would help me
in the future with investing or working
with management teams. So, I went to
Warren and said, you know, I'd like to
be CEO of, you know, Pampered Chef,
which I was working with at the time.
And then what I saw was there's a lot of
opportunity in that business. It had a
strong brand. It had a strong channel.
It just had been under managed. And so,
the transition from chairman to CEO was
really, I think for a lot of people,
surprising, right? Very seldom do you
see investors go into operating roles.
Um but for me, I really felt like it was
going to be the future of investing was
going to be operating, and I would be a
much better investor if I went and got
that experience directly um and gained
that credibility, the empathy, the
connection with these leaders that would
resonate with sellers in the future,
resonate with management teams, and
definitely have seen that play out at
Cambrek, as well.
>> As you look at those different um
connections with the company from
investor to chairman to CEO, how did you
think about going in for the first time
and laying out communicating what a plan
would be?
>> Yeah, so I always think the best way to
go in is to go in open-minded with more
questions than answers. I think
investors usually come in with answers.
Here's our 90-day plan. This is what
we're going to go do. And I think the
reality is you don't actually get the
best outcomes in doing that. We as we
start at Cambrek with like listen and
learning. You know, how do you actually
listen to people in the organization?
How do you understand what's going on?
How do you ask the questions that are
going to help you be smarter, but also
further the conversation? And if you do
that well, you actually get to a better
outcome. You can co-create something
that's really meaningful in terms of the
strategy and the direction and the
focus. And that is far more powerful
than coming in with a plan or a
direction in what you're doing.
>> What was different from what you
expected at Pampered Chef?
>> When I came in, I had been working with
the business for about a year. So, I'd
spent time learning, listening, and I
had a pretty strong view at that stage
of like what we needed to go do. And I
told Warren it would take me a year,
maybe 2 years to get this thing like
really humming. You know, it had been in
decline for about a decade, so it was a
big turnaround that I needed to go do.
And it ended up taking you nearly 4
years to do it. And the reality is is I
think everything is harder in operating
than it seems. And so, even though I
knew what needed to go be done, I had
the strategy in my mind, I knew I needed
to go get the people on board, build the
culture, it's a lot harder than you
expect. And usually that's because it's
all involved people, and people are
really tough, right? You hire the wrong
people, you've got to change them out.
Or you've got to work on culture and
retention, which that doesn't get
changed overnight if, you know, you've
had challenges in that in the past. And
then you've got to go invest in people
getting up to speed and learning sort of
new tools, new practices, new spaces,
and then you've got to build all this
together. And so, to me that was a huge
surprise, very humbling, but I think
it's probably actually not dissimilar
from how most investors think, right?
Like, "Oh, let's take margins from 10%
to 14%." You know, that's one click in
my spreadsheet, but in reality in a
business, that takes a lot more work to
actually go do. And there's a lot of
missteps or mistakes and learnings along
the way to get to there.
>> So, as you progress, you spend this time
as a CEO, you can imagine being at
Berkshire for a career, and just going
in and working with different companies,
larger companies, Berkshire. At what
point time did you decide you wanted to
go do your own thing instead of doing it
within Berkshire?
>> Yeah, so I was nearing sort of the
conclusion of the turnaround at Pampered
Chef. We had the business in a good
place. I had met my now co-founder Brian
Humphrey, he had joined me as CFO there.
We were very well aligned from a vision
and values perspective. And what I saw
at that sort of stage was I could be at
Berkshire forever. I'd have an amazing
time there. It's a remarkable company,
there's nothing like it, and I don't
think there ever will be. But it was
getting very big in terms of capital.
So, it had 150 billion in cash at the
time, you know, now it's 300 billion
plus. It's very hard to move the needle
with that size of check. And what I saw
was actually what Berkshire had done 30
or 40 years ago was actually more
interesting to me. Buying businesses
like Benjamin Moore or others, where you
could actually partner with them, help
them accelerate the growth. And also
what I've seen in the market at the time
was there was just a growing group of
families and founders who wanted
something different. They didn't want to
sell to traditional private equity. They
wanted a Berkshire-like home, but they
were just too small. And so there was
this opportunity like in that moment to
build something that was unique and
different that I think was solving a
pain point. And so for me it was, yes, I
could stay here and be happy and
probably forever, but there's also this
opportunity to build something special
and unique that you know I think was was
really
sort of differentiated in the moment.
>> When Brian and you decided you're going
to do this,
what did you lay out as the core tenets
of your philosophy having pulled from
your experiences at Berkshire?
>> Yeah, there were a few things that
resonated with us that really were
important. One is long-term thinking and
a long-term structure. So I think often
times long-term thinking conflicts with
structure and so having those two things
together was very important to us. And
that very much was you know paramount to
Berkshire and I think very unique and
special and something we wanted to
replicate at Cambrek. Second was
providing sort of that operating lens
and that operating expertise. So we had
built what is now the Cambrek business
system from the ground up learning from
greats like
Marmon and Toyota and Trans Diamond
others and really taking those and
re-sort of applying them for mid-size
companies. And that tenant of that
investor operator mindset in partnership
was really powerful. And then lastly was
just this partnership mindset of like
working with families and founders and
coming alongside them. I think so much
in traditional private equity is you
know we you get told what to do or you
know go drive this or hit this you know
plan versus how do we co-create and
build something special and unique. And
that partnership mentality is like so
core and critical to how to how we
operate and how we think.
>> What did you do different structurally
from the way private equity
traditionally runs?
>> Yeah, so we did a longer-term structure.
So, you know, it has a longer-term
horizon, which is beneficial for us. We
have 15 plus years in our structure. And
the benefit of that is that one, it
self-selects investors who are long-term
and oriented long-term oriented, which
is very beneficial. And it's unique for
owners. So, owners who say, "Look, I'm
you concerned with the the three to
four-year treadmill of private equity."
It gives them comfort that their
business isn't going to be sold bought
and sold and bought and sold so sort of
quickly. And it's that longer-term
horizon that allows our management teams
to really focus on how do I build this
business for decades, not how do I build
this business for a quick flip.
>> And what did you find when you went into
the market with that structure?
>> Yes, from an investor perspective, you
know, it's obviously there's some
investors it just isn't a fit for. Like
it doesn't match their structure, their
duration, their liquidity needs, which
we understand. Um but I think what it
really we really saw is there was a a
group of investors who were immediately
resonated with them. And it was aligned
with how they think about building
businesses as well, which was natural.
And what we said to investors is it
doesn't mean you won't get any capital
along the way. So, you know, there's
always going to be opportunities. Um our
businesses we don't put a lot a lot of
leverage on them. Um and so there'll be
some businesses that we exit, but a lot
of our businesses will generate a fair
amount of cash because they don't have a
lot of leverage. And then we can return
capital. We have a business JAM test.
We've owned it three years. You know, we
forexed the earnings in the business
over that period and then we just sort
of returned um you know, our initial
capital to investors. And we still own
our 70% you know, plus of the business.
And so that I think is a great model
where yes, there's liquidity. It's not
the same as an exit, but that business
is compounding at 20% plus a year. We'd
rather continue to own that business
rather than sort of exit it.
>> How did you take the long-term nature of
the structure
and tell a story to the people you
wanted to partner with? So, it could be
the families, it could be the investors
um to really encapsulate that idea of
partnership?
>> there's a few things that we highlight
is as the structure is important, but
it's one part of like the three-legged
stool. So, there's a long-term structure
that allows us to invest in these
high-quality businesses. There's our
Cambre community, which is how we get to
know companies and we build
relationships over the long term. And
then there's the business system about
as we add value. And they all get
mutually reinforced and powerful
together. So, by having that longer term
structure, our management teams can
think longer term. By our management
teams thinking longer term, we can drive
above-average returns. By having our
Cambre
business system, we can use it in our
community. By having that in our
community, we get to know owners and
CEOs well ahead of any potential
partnership. And when those things start
to really compound on each other, you
get the real value of it. And so, for
us, it has been tough to like
communicate that story because it's not
a simple easy one. It actually is very
interconnected. But our belief and our
competitive advantage is it is those
things, and that becomes stronger and
stronger over time and harder for
someone else to come in and replicate.
>> the Cambre community.
What did you build to generate that
community?
>> Yeah, so when I started as CEO of
Pampered Chef, it was very lonely. I had
to go out and, you know, meet with
owners and and meet with other
executives to really understand, how do
you manage a business effectively and
well? And when I was doing that, I
thought, "Wow, it'd be so great to have
a resource, someone who could come
alongside me and say, 'This is what a
great strategic planning process looks
like, or this is how you can improve
your executive hiring skills.'" And so,
when I started
sort of that journey, I really realized
that there was this need to help owners,
that they wanted to learn and grow, and
CEOs in particular. And so, when started
Cambre, we sort of brought that idea
forward with this opportunity to get to
know owners and CEOs over time. And so,
we built the Cambre community to be sort
of that home that we wanted to have in
terms of learning and growing together.
You know, now we have 4,000 CEOs in the
community and owners and C-suite
executives, where we're helping them
with their business. We're really taking
a step back and saying, you know, this
is what a great KPI process looks like.
These are what the best benchmarks are.
And that community relationship has been
really powerful and helpful for us
because we learn about new spaces, we
get to know businesses, but most
importantly, these companies get to know
us. And we build trust and credibility.
And the reality is my view is that the
world is becoming much more focused on
relationship investing than sort of
transaction. So, all of our investments
have come through direct relationships.
Um four of our seven have come through
the community, but what we're doing is
we're building goodwill, we're building
trust. And even if the companies aren't
ever going to take a partner or not
interested in a partner, what we find is
they become great ambassadors for us.
And so, they share, you know, about
Cambrek with their friends, other CEOs.
And that's been been incredibly
powerful.
>> It's easy to see how that would work at
4,000. How do you get from zero to
>> It's a great question. So, we started
with our first program called Build with
Cambrek. Uh CEOs applied to it, and in
